title: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, large shells similar to small ones

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, large shells similar to small ones

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, recognisable by continued similarity: the large many-chambered shell has the same shape as the smaller, younger shell.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}, recognised by self-similarity of young and old shells

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The logarithmic spiral is easily recognisable in typical cases (and especially where the spire makes more than one visible revolution about the pole), by its fundamental property of continued similarity: that is to say, by reason of the fact that the big many-chambered shell is of just the same shape as the smaller and younger shell

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Logarithmic spiral of foraminiferal shells”. Scope: nautiloid and other spiral Foraminifera

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}, recognised by self-similarity of young and old shells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-04: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.79

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a direct model-selection problem with clear geometric variables and standard methods. Public images and scans should resolve the assertion for a substantial, though not exhaustive, sample of spiral Foraminifera.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit logarithmic and rival spiral models to chamber centroids and shell outlines across ontogenetic whorls, and test scale-invariant similarity of successive stages. Stable logarithmic parameters and superior fit support the claim; systematic parameter drift or better rival fits refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Internal chambers require tomography rather than exterior photographs.

Available scans may overrepresent conspicuous taxa.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Continued similarity is exactly the measurement Thompson uses to recognize a logarithmic spiral, and fusulinid outlines already record shape at each whorl. Image atlases extend the test to many other coiled genera, though not as precomputed spiral angles and not evenly across benthic families. Fitting a constant angle against alternatives is a standard morphometric job on the fusulinid file and a slower image-measurement job elsewhere, so the law is testable now for a large subset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On axial sections and 3D whorls, estimate the spiral angle at successive chambers and test self-similarity by superimposing younger and older outlines after scaling. A logarithmic spiral is supported when the angle is constant and scaled outlines coincide within measurement error; a changing angle, or a better fit by an Archimedean or multistage spiral, would refute it for that shell.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The open landmark series is fusulinid, a subset of the nautiloid and other spiral foraminifera named in the claim.

Trochospiral tests need a 3D angle; equatorial photographs alone underdetermine the spiral.
